questions.q: what do we learn about Hannibal from these opening words?
points: he was the son of Hamilcar
he was a Carthaginian / came from Carthage

questions.q: why do you think Nepos ends the opening sentence with this word?
points: emphatic final position of Carthaginiensis
it reminds the reader straight away that Hannibal is Rome’s great enemy
his nationality is part of his identity, like his father’s name

questions.q: why do you think Nepos adds these words?
points: he interrupts his own sentence (parenthesis) to insist that Rome’s superiority is beyond question
it reassures his Roman readers
before he goes on to praise Rome’s enemy so highly

questions.q: how does Nepos make his praise of Hannibal acceptable to a Roman reader?
points: he first states that Rome surpassed all nations (omnes gentes) in courage
he adds that no one doubts it (quod nemo dubitat)
litotes non est infitiandum makes the praise sound reluctant, forced on him by the facts
Hannibal excels in prudentia (skill / judgement) while Rome excels in fortitudine (courage), so he is never said to be braver than the Romans
the balanced tanto … quanto ranks Hannibal among generals only as high as Rome is ranked among nations
questions.guidance: Accept any four. Each point must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: explain in your own words what Nepos thinks might have happened.
points: if Hannibal had not been weakened by the jealousy of his own people at home
he would apparently have been able to defeat the Romans
Nepos is careful to say only that it ‘seems’ so (videtur)

questions.q: what does Nepos say about Hannibal’s record against Rome and the reason he did not win the war?
points: whenever he fought the Romans in Italy
he always came away the winner
he was weakened at home
by the jealousy of his own citizens
otherwise he seems to have been able to defeat the Romans
the criticism / disparagement of many people
overcame the courage / ability of one man

questions.q: explain in your own words how Hannibal treated the hatred of Rome that he inherited.
points: it was his father’s hatred of the Romans
it came to him like an inheritance
he kept it / held on to it faithfully
he would sooner give up his life than give up that hatred

questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s hatred of Rome seem part of who he is?
points: metaphor of an inheritance (hereditate relictum): the hatred is passed down like property in a will
paternum: it is his father’s hatred, part of his family
so Hannibal was born into it rather than choosing it

questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise Hannibal’s determination in these lines?
points: even when driven from his homeland (patria pulsus)
and dependent on others’ resources (alienarum opum indigeret)
emphatic numquam: he never once stopped
animo bellare: he fought Rome in spirit even without an army
the chapter ends on cum Romanis, his lifelong enemy
questions.guidance: Accept any three. Each point must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: explain in your own words what Nepos says about Philip.
points: Nepos says he will pass over Philip
Hannibal made Philip an enemy of the Romans
without being there in person / from a distance

questions.q: why do you think Nepos says that he will ‘pass over’ Philip?
points: praeteritio: he says he will leave Philip out, yet names him all the same
it slips in one more example of Hannibal turning a king against Rome
while seeming to hurry on to the main story of Antiochus

questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise the strength of Hannibal’s influence on Antiochus?
points: incendit: fire metaphor, Hannibal sets the king alight
tanta cupiditate: ‘so great’ a desire
bellandi is held back to the end of the clause, so ‘war’ lands with weight
usque a rubro mari … Italiae: the planned war stretches across almost the whole known world
Italiae is the final word, so the target comes as a climax
questions.guidance: Accept any four. Each point must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what part of the world does Nepos mean by this?
points: the far eastern edge of Antiochus’ empire / the waters south and east of Arabia

questions.lemma: ad quem cum legati … segregari vidisset
questions.q: describe the Roman envoys’ scheme and what came of it.
points: Roman envoys came to Antiochus
to find out his intentions
they worked through secret plots
to make the king suspicious of Hannibal
as if he had been bribed by the Romans
and now thought differently from before
their plan succeeded
Hannibal found out about it
he saw that he was being shut out of the king’s inner counsels

questions.q: why is this phrase ironic?
points: the Romans want the king to think Hannibal has been bribed by them
yet the Romans are the ones acting corruptly, secretly deceiving the king
Hannibal himself remains loyal

questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s position at court vivid?
points: segregari: literally ‘separated from the flock’
interioribus consiliis pictures an inner circle of advisers
so Hannibal is seen left outside it, cut off from the king

questions.q: explain in your own words how Hannibal began his conversation with the king.
points: he spoke at length / said a great deal
about his loyalty to the king
about his hatred of the Romans
then he added the story that follows

questions.q: why do you think Nepos uses this title for the god?
points: it is the formal title of Jupiter used in official worship
the grand, ceremonial language makes the scene solemn and sacred
so the hatred that comes out of it seems approved by the gods
giving the Carthaginian god Jupiter’s name makes the scene familiar to a Roman reader

questions.q: what impression of the young Hannibal do we get, and how does Nepos create it?
points: he is eager to go: libenter (‘gladly’)
he begs his father: petere coepissem
role reversal: the father makes the offer, but the son ends up pleading
ne dubitaret ducere: he presses his father not to hesitate
from the start he wanted to be a soldier
questions.guidance: Accept any three. Each point must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: how does Nepos make Hamilcar’s reply forceful?
points: direct speech gives his own words
the bargain is made in a single short sentence, like a contract
faciam comes first: a decisive one-word answer
fidem: the key word ‘pledge / good faith’, which Antiochus now doubts

questions.q: how does Nepos make the taking of the oath solemn and private?
points: simul: it follows at once, with no time to reconsider
ad aram: at the altar, a sacred place
where the sacrifice had begun (sacrificare instituerat)
ceteris remotis: everyone else is sent away, so it is a bond between father and son alone
eamque … tenentem: the boy’s hand on the altar is a physical, sacred gesture
iurare iussit: the oath is commanded
questions.guidance: Accept any four. Each point must refer to the Latin.

questions.lemma: numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore
questions.q: explain in your own words what Hannibal swore.
points: that he would never
be a friend of the Romans / on friendly terms with Rome

questions.q: how does Hannibal stress his faithfulness to the oath?
points: id ego iusiurandum: the oath is placed first, with the emphatic pronoun ego
patri datum: it was given to his father, so it is a family duty
usque ad hanc aetatem: he has kept it from boyhood to old age
ita conservavi: he has kept it so completely
questions.guidance: Accept any three. Each point must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: how does Hannibal show confidence in his own value?
points: te ipsum frustraberis: he bluntly tells a king that he would only fool himself
he says Antiochus must put him in command of the war
principem is the last word of his speech: a claim to leadership
the contrast with the earlier advice to hide peace plans shows he is useful only for war against Rome

questions.q: what does Nepos mean by these words, and why does he add them?
points: ‘at the age we mentioned’: when Hannibal was nine
qua diximus: Nepos steps back into his own narrative after Hannibal’s speech
it rounds off the story (ring structure) and returns to the start of his career

questions.q: describe in detail how Hannibal came to swear his oath.
points: while the sacrifice was being carried out
Hamilcar asked if he wanted to go with him to the camp
Hannibal gladly accepted
he begged his father not to hesitate to take him
Hamilcar agreed, if Hannibal gave him the pledge he asked for
he led him to the altar
everyone else was sent away
Hannibal held the altar
he swore that he would never be a friend of the Romans

questions.q: why was Spain so important to Carthage at this time?
points: Carthage had lost Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica to Rome after the First Punic War
Spain had silver mines
and manpower
it gave Carthage the resources for a second war

questions.q: how does Nepos stress that Hannibal’s appointment was legitimate?
points: the army itself gave him supreme command (exercitus … ad eum detulit)
publice comprobatum est: it was officially approved by the state
detulit … delatum: the same verb links the soldiers’ choice to the city’s approval
so the command was given to him, with no hint that he seized it by force

questions.q: what happened after Hamilcar’s death?
points: Hasdrubal took over as commander
Hannibal was put in charge of all the cavalry

questions.lemma: minor quinque et viginti annis natus
questions.q: why do you think Nepos gives Hannibal’s age so precisely here?
points: it spells out how young he was: not yet twenty-five
the reader is struck that so young a man commanded a whole army
it marks him out as exceptional from the very start

questions.q: what did Hannibal achieve after he became commander?
points: he was not yet twenty-five
within the next three years
he conquered all the peoples of Spain
he took Saguntum by force
a city allied to Rome
he raised three very large armies
he sent one to Africa
he left one in Spain with his brother Hasdrubal
he led the third into Italy himself

questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s achievements in Spain seem astonishing?
points: hyperbole omnes gentes Hispaniae: every people of Spain
proximo triennio: all within three years
asyndeton: three achievements follow with no connecting words, giving rapid, relentless activity
vi expugnavit: Saguntum taken by force
superlative maximos: the armies were very large
questions.guidance: Accept any three. Each point must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what later became of this Hasdrubal?
points: he held Spain for Carthage until 208 BC
he led an army into Italy to reinforce Hannibal
he was defeated and killed at the Metaurus (207 BC)

questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s own army stand out?
points: tricolon: the three armies are dealt out in three balanced clauses (unum … alterum … tertium)
the climax is the third army, the one he leads himself (secum duxit)
its destination, in Italiam, is the most important

questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise Hannibal’s success on the march?
points: quacumque: wherever he went
cum omnibus incolis: he fought every people he met
emphatic negative neminem nisi victum: no exceptions, everyone was beaten
short clauses / asyndeton give a sense of speed
questions.guidance: Accept any three. Each point must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what legend lies behind this reference?
points: Hercules was said to have crossed the Alps
on his way back from Spain
with the cattle of Geryon
the Graian Alps were linked with his name

questions.lemma: ad Alpes posteaquam … vix poterat repere
questions.q: describe Hannibal’s crossing of the Alps.
points: the Alps separate Italy from Gaul
no one had crossed them with an army before him
except the Greek Hercules
so the pass is still called the Graian Pass
he cut down the Alpine tribes
who tried to stop him crossing
he opened up the terrain
he built roads
a fully laden elephant could now go
where before a single unarmed man could barely crawl

essays.q: how does Nepos praise Hannibal while keeping his Roman readers on his side?
points: he begins by granting that Rome surpassed every nation in courage, a point no one doubts
his praise of Hannibal is presented as a fact that cannot be denied, so it seems forced on him
Hannibal is given skill and judgement, Rome courage, so neither side is insulted
Hannibal was never beaten in Italy, a bold claim, softened by the cautious ‘seems’
his defeat is blamed on jealousy at home, so Rome’s victory does not have to be explained away
the hatred he inherited from his father makes him a formidable but understandable enemy
even in exile he never stopped fighting Rome, which shows how dangerous he remained

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal’s hatred of Rome as the driving force of his life?
points: Hannibal is defeated by the spite of many, but his own spirit stays unbroken
his hatred is an inheritance from his father, handed down like property
he would sooner lose his life than his hatred
even as an exile depending on others he kept fighting Rome in spirit
he turned Philip of Macedon into Rome’s enemy without even meeting him
he fired the most powerful king of the age with a desire for war
the planned war stretches from the Red Sea to Italy, showing the reach of his hatred

essays.q: how does Nepos contrast the Romans with Hannibal?
points: the Roman envoys work in secret, through hidden plots
they try to make the king believe Hannibal has been bribed, when they are the ones deceiving him
their scheme works and Hannibal is shut out of the king’s inner circle
Hannibal finds out and acts openly, going straight to the king
he speaks frankly about his loyalty and his hatred of Rome
he tells the story of his childhood in his own words
the solemn sacrifice to Jupiter sets his sincerity against Roman deceit

essays.q: how does Nepos make the scene of the oath vivid and solemn?
points: Hannibal tells the story himself, in direct speech
he was only a small boy of nine
Hamilcar was setting out as commander for Spain
the scene is set at a sacrifice to Jupiter, Best and Greatest
the boy is eager and begs to go with his father
Hamilcar sets a stark condition: a pledge
the oath is sworn at the altar, in private, with the boy’s hand on it, never to be Rome’s friend

essays.q: how does Nepos present the relationship between Hamilcar and the young Hannibal?
points: Hamilcar asks his son rather than ordering him
the boy gladly accepts and even begs to be taken
Hamilcar makes his agreement conditional on a pledge
father and son are alone at the altar, others sent away
the oath is given to the father, so the hatred is a family bond
Hannibal has kept the oath to his father all his life
the father’s influence shapes his whole future, even his advice to a king

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as a natural leader?
points: Hannibal claims he has kept his oath all his life, so his word can be trusted
he speaks confidently and tactfully to a king
he tells Antiochus he would fool himself if he did not make him commander
his speech ends with a claim to leadership
he went to Spain with his father at the age of nine
he was put in charge of the whole cavalry while still young
the army chose him as commander and the state approved

essays.lemma: ex his unum … in Italiamque pervenit
essays.q: how does Nepos make the crossing of the Alps seem a heroic achievement?
points: Hannibal leads the third army into Italy himself
he crosses the Pyrenees and defeats every people on the way
the Alps are a great natural barrier between Gaul and Italy
only the legendary Hercules had crossed them with an army before
he cuts down the Alpine tribes who try to stop him
he opens up the land and builds roads
a laden elephant can now go where an unarmed man could barely crawl

essays.q: how does Nepos convey the speed of Hannibal’s rise and his early successes?
points: two commanders die in quick succession, dealt with in a few words
Hannibal is given the cavalry, then the supreme command
the army chooses him and the state approves
he is not yet twenty-five
he conquers all of Spain within three years
he takes Saguntum and raises three huge armies
he crosses the Pyrenees and defeats everyone in his way
